reading.rtitle: Shall, and the Words That Do the Work
paras: Nothing in a commercial contract is neutral, and the smallest words carry the most weight. A party that shall deliver has undertaken to deliver; a party that may deliver has been given a choice and nothing more. The distinction looks obvious written down like this, and it produces litigation every year, because drafters use shall for obligations, for conditions and occasionally for the future, and a reader has to work out which one is meant from the rest of the sentence. Anyone who has looked at a badly drafted clause knows the feeling: the sentence is perfectly grammatical and nobody can say what it requires.

The reform movement in English-language drafting argues that shall should be abolished and replaced with must for duties and with is entitled to for rights. Several jurisdictions now require it in legislation. Commercial practice has not followed, partly out of habit and partly because must reads as aggressive to some clients, which is a bad reason and a real one. What has changed is the expectation that a clause states clearly who owes what to whom: the supplier must notify, the buyer is entitled to inspect, neither party may assign without consent. A clause written that way survives translation, and this one matters more than lawyers admit, because the contract will be read by people whose first language is not English.

The other half of the problem is negative. A clause that says a party shall not do something is a prohibition; a clause that says a party is not required to do something removes a duty and grants no permission at all. Most disputes about obligation are really disputes about which of those two a sentence contains. Read the modal first, then the subject, then whatever exception has been carved out of it, and most of a clause becomes readable in one pass. What is left after that is the negotiation, and that is a different skill.

listenings.text: People assume that in-house counsel read contracts from the first page, and I have never once done that. I go to the back. I read the governing law, the termination clause and the liability cap first, in that order, because those three tell me what happens on the worst day, and everything at the front is only interesting if we get to the worst day. Then I read every sentence with a modal verb in it and I mark them in two colours: one for what we owe them, one for what they owe us. It takes twenty minutes and it has saved me from signing three agreements I would still be explaining today. The thing I look hardest for is the clause that removes a duty without granting a permission, because that is the one everybody misreads, including me, twice.

I have been teaching contract drafting for eleven years, and the argument about shall is the one that makes previously calm people shout. Here is where I have landed. Shall is not evil. The problem is that a single word is being asked to do four different jobs in the same document, and no reader can tell which job it is doing without stopping to think. Must is not aggressive, it is simply unfamiliar, and unfamiliar wears off in about a week. What actually persuades a sceptical partner is not the style guide. It is opening their own contract, finding the fourth or fifth shall on the page, and asking them, out loud, whether that sentence creates a duty or describes something that will happen. Half the time they cannot answer, and that is the end of the argument.
